summary:
Región de Valparaíso stands under the national framework of Chile. Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019: adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, while applicants aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents. People under 14 cannot use the statute, which nevertheless recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates have offered a third sex option for intersex children since 2006. No legal ban exists on medically unnecessary interventions on intersex minors; the Health Minister published non-binding intersex-affirming guidance in 2023.

Transphobic violence remains documented nationally. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime, with an acquaintance perpetrator confessing. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, and the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, while the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Regional conditions in Región de Valparaíso are not benign. Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report records that the region concentrated 51.32% of national recorded anti-LGBTI discrimination cases in 2024, an increase of 80.93% over 2023. In 2025 recorded cases fell only in Valparaíso and Metropolitana while all other regions rose; Movilh reads this pattern as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ themes have less visibility.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.
tangentialFactors:
Chile's national legal position sits at the more developed end of its region: a comprehensive gender-recognition statute based on self-determination since 2019, marriage equality with full adoption rights since March 2022, and a 2012 anti-discrimination statute whose protections were extended to gender expression in 2018.

Article 365 of the Penal Code set a higher age of consent of 18 for male homosexual acts until 2022; the Constitutional Court upheld the provision by a 5-5 vote in August 2018 and Law 21,483 abolished it in August 2022, equalising the age of consent. A 2020 family-court decision recognised two women as parents of a child born through assisted reproduction, and a 2025 criminal court issued the country's first conviction in that field.

The CEI 57 report approved on 15 May 2025 is a recommendation without legal force, but it marks a live parliamentary appetite for reversing parts of the current framework, including hormonal treatment restrictions for minors and the school circular.

Recorded discrimination data for Región de Valparaíso runs on a full per-region and per-commune series from 2002 to 2025 in Movilh's reporting, so the 2024 concentration and the 2025 movement can be checked against the longer series rather than read as a single-year spike.
localsOnly:
Región de Valparaíso hosted the first Encuentro de Oficinas Municipales de Diversidad in 2022, followed by the second gathering in Melipilla in 2023 and the third in Concepción in 2024.

San Antonio, a comuna within Región de Valparaíso, was among the founding members of the Red de Municipalidades por la Diversidad, Inclusión y No Discriminación, created in 2014 as a network of municipalities running LGBTIQA+ offices or programmes and grown beyond 60 municipalities by 2024.

Residents have been able to register a civil union with the national police since April 2016, when the first Carabinero contracted one with a same-sex partner, and the Chilean Army formally incorporated its first transgender member in 2020; the armed forces admit LGBT personnel.

Residents have access to the Ministry of Health-run support programme in medical centres and to Crece con Orgullo, running since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17, alongside the surgery and hormone funding available in the public system since 2013 and the social-name registration rule issued in 2011.
outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of the Constitutional Court's 9 April 2025 ruling on the 'over 14 years old' wording is unresolved beyond the single case before it; whether family courts have since applied the reasoning more widely is not sourced here.

No source in this inventory reports enforcement outcomes for the Gendarmería de Chile detention protocol inside Región de Valparaíso, including how often placement by assumed gender has been refused or how the standing committee has handled complaints.

Regional data on hate-crime prosecutions, sentences and Zamudio Law complaints in Región de Valparaíso, as distinct from recorded discrimination complaints, is not sourced; Movilh's figures count recorded cases rather than convictions.

Whether the annulment of section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law has translated into funded hormone therapy for minors in this region's public facilities, and how Circular 7 of June 2024 is applied in practice by local clinicians, remain unresolved on the available sources.

No source addresses airport or border screening, document inspection or facilities access for trans travellers arriving in Región de Valparaíso; the entry rules cited cover asylum and non-refoulement rather than routine visitor processing.
